## Segmental duplications drive NAHR

:::{.center}
:::{.small}

- Segmental duplications (SDs) recruit NAHR
- ~5% of human genome
- High identity (>~95%)
- Large (>~10kbp)

## NAHR elements and risk

<br>

:::{.small}
:::{.center}

| Homologous element | Min. Seq. identitiy | Min. length | 
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Segmental duplication (SD) | 90% | 1kbp |
| Long interspersed nuclear element (LINE) | 96% | smaller than 1kbp |
| Human endogenous retro virus (HERV) | 93% | 3kbp | 

<br>


- Risk $\propto$ length & sequence identity
- Risk $\frac{1}{\propto}$ distance between elements

:::
:::

::: notes

citation? probably one of the SV mech papers

:::

## NAHR summary

<br>

:::{.center}

- Recombination at homologous, but non-matching loci
- Breakpoints have large homology
- Example: Smith-Magenis syndrome
- Relatively high reurrency

:::

## Chronic myeloid leukemia fusion

![](./img/dup-trp.inv-dup.png){fig-align="center"}

## NHEJ summary

<br>

:::{.center}

- Imperfect repair of double strand DNA break
- Minimal homology at breakpoints
- Example: BCR-ABL1 fusion CML
- *Usually* low recurrency

:::

## Temple syndrome

:::{.center}

<br>

- BIR SV: CHR 14 DUP-TRP/INV-DUP
- Symptoms
  - Intellectual disabilities
  - Early onset puberty

:::

## BIR summary

- Replication template switching due to microhomology
- Breakpoints show microhomology
- Example: Temple syndrome; CHR 14 DUP-TRP/INV-DUP
- Low recurrency

Template switching during replication

## Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease

<br>

:::{.center}

- Mechanism: CHR X DUP; PLP1 gene
- Symptoms:
  - Involuntary movements
  - Developmental delays
:::

## FoSTeS summary

:::{.center}

<br>

- Template switching from one replication fork to another
- Breakpoints have microhomology
- Example: Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease
- Low recurrency

:::

## SV mechanisms

:::{.small}
:::{.center}


| Mechanism | When | Recurrency | Breakpoint homology | Ex. pathology |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| NAHR | Recombination | Relatively high | Large | Smith–Magenis syndrome; DEL on CHR 17, RAI1 gene |
| NHEJ  | Repair | Low | None or small | Chronic Myeloid Leukemia; FUSION of BCR-ABL genes |
| BIR | Replication | Low | Small | Temple syndrome; DEL on CHR 14 |
| FoSTeS | Replication | Low | Small | Pelizaeus-Merzbacher; DUP CHR X, PLP1 gene | 

:::
:::

::: notes

- NAHR pathology: Mechanisms underlying structural variant formation in genomic disorde
- BIR pathology: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41594-025-01644-z#Sec5 table1
- NHEJ pathology: Distinct pattern of genomic breakpoints in CML and BCR::ABL1-positive ALL: analysis of 971 patients
- FoSTeS pathology: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2685756/

:::


## SV mechanism research gaps

<br>

:::{.center}

- Calling *dependent* SVs
- Calling SVs using sequencing and mechanism models jointly
- Which mechanisms are most frequent?
- Association of mechanisms and pathologies

:::

## Dependent SVs and mechanisms

:::{.center}
:::{.small}
- A single NHEJ event may produce multiple SVs
- NAHR rarely produces insertions
- Breakpoint sequence could rule out SV dependence
  - E.g., INS+DEL with large homology at DEL breakpoints
:::


![](./img/nhej.webp){fig-align="center" width="75%"}

## Complexity of 1bp context SNVs

:::{.center}

<br>

- gnomAD considers SNVs with 1bp context
  - A**C**G -> A**A**G OR A**T**G OR A**G**G
- $4^3=64$ possible 3-mers
- 3 possible SNVs per 3-mer
- Total 3-mer SNVs is $64\cdot 3=192$



:::

Is SNV functional class enriched with rare (singleton) events?
:::


![](./img/gnomad-f1cdefgh.png){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

## MAPS

:::{.center}
:::{.small}

- MAPS: Mutability adjusted proportion of singletons
- Aggregate singletons within SNV functional classes (e.g., pLoF or missense)
- MAPS $\approx$ Observed singleton prop. $-\text{ }f$(expected singleton prop.)
- MAPS > 0: more singletons observed than expected
<!-- - Expected: derived from non-coding regions, weighted by mutation rate (freq.) -->

![](./img/maps.png){fig-align="center" width="30%"}

:::
:::

## LOEUF

:::{.small}
:::{.center}

- LOEUF: Loss-of-function observed expected upper bound fraction
- Goal: mesaure intolerance to pLoF
- Approach: score genes by pLoF SNV proportion
- Metric: #Obs. pLoF SNVs / #Exp. pLoF SNVs; take upper bound CI

![](./img/loeuf-ex.png){fig-align="center"}

:::
:::

## SV SNP LD

:::{.center}
:::{.small}

- **LD**: linkage disequilibrium
  - $r^2 \approx 1 \rightarrow$ non-random co-occurence
  - $r^2 \approx 0 \rightarrow$ random co-occurence
- Here, LD measured for SVs and nearby SNPs

:::

## SV partial element overlap

- Log enrichment: $<0 \rightarrow$ less overlap than expected
- RVIS: residual variation intolerance score (functional variant intolernace)
  - $\uparrow RVIS \rightarrow$ $\uparrow$ variant tolerance

![](./img/1kg_sv_sr-2ab.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- left: important elements less constrained for DELs 
- left: higher VAF -> lower chance of element overlap
- right: DELs are usually more constrained than other SV types
:::

## LD of lead eQTL SNPs and SVs

:::{.small}
:::{.center}
- Hypothesis: sig. GWAS SNPs associated with SVs
- Denom: # expected SVs in LD with lead eQTL
  - Swap SV into another SV region with similar properties (e.g., VAF)
  - Restrict LD search space to +/- Xbps from TSS
  - Constrain haplotype length ($r^2$ [$\downarrow r^2 \rightarrow \uparrow$ haplotype len.])
  - Is lead eQTL SNP in haplotype length? (yes $\rightarrow+1$)
:::
:::

:::notes
- When haplotype length is constrained, # SVs in LD with lead eQTL SNP greater than expected
- The association of lead eQTL SNPs and SV is more likely the large the SV
- Yes, it's possible that traits associated lead eQTL SNPs may actually explained by SVs
:::

![](./img/1kg_sv_sr-2e.png){fig-align="center"}

## Long read (LR) depth and size

:::{.center}
:::{.small}
- ~16.9x median coverage
  - $\uparrow$ coverage $\rightarrow$ $\uparrow$ sensitivity to mosaic variants
- ~20.3kbp median read length
  - 100x larger than typical short-read
  - SVs can be contained in a single read
- LR is single-end, not paired-end
:::
:::

![](./img/1kg_sv_lr-1b.png){fig-align="center"}

## Augmented graph SV analysis

:::{.center}

1. Align to 3 different references (GRCh38, CHM13, and HPRC)

:::{.small}
- Linear: GRCh38 and CHM13
- Graph: HPRC

## Augmented graph SV analysis

3. Create pseudo-haplotypes

- Pool SVs by caller
- Create haplotypes such that no SVs overlap within haplotype
- Use bcftools consensus to resolve sequence

## Genotype v haplotype

:::{.center}
:::{.small}
- Genotype: which alleles present and how many?
  - Ex: A/A homozygous SNP at CHR4:123456bp $\rightarrow$ genotype = "1/1"
- Haplotype: which alleles physically linked on singular chromosome?
  - Ex: SNPs at bp 4 (C>A) & 7 (A>C)  are "phased" to same physical chromosome
:::
:::

## SV sub-classes

:::{.center}
:::{.small}

- Classes resolved by SV annotator (SVAN)
- VNTR: variable number tandem repeat
- ALU: ~300bp mobile element

![](./img/1kg_sv_lr-3a.png){fig-align="center"}

:::
:::

::: notes
- VNTR is most common SV class for both DEL and INS
- DEL would remove some section of tandem repeats
- INS would add tandem repeats
- High MAF suggests these variants are not only common in magnitude, but shared across individuals
- Aside from VNTR, most other SV classes have low AF
:::

## INV sub-classes

<br>

![](./img/1kg_sv_lr-3b.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- INV DUP more common than simple INV, tend to be smaller than other INV types
- Overall, beyond mechanism and breakpoints, SV sub-classes have characteristic lengths and AF
:::

## L1 transduction activity

:::{.center}
:::{.small}
Transduction: element is copied and inserted elsewhere
:::

![](./img/1kg_sv_lr-3a-l1.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}
![](./img/1kg_sv_lr-4a.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"}

:::

:::notes
- L1: mobile element w/ characteristic ~6kbp length. includes a repeat region
- Takeaway: some mobile elements are more active than others and adjancent seq copied along is biased to the origin of element
- Tail transduction bias except for 3rd origin loci
- Not in GRCh38 nor CHM13 means it was in the graph genome
- Takeaway 2: Prior reports have many of these elements as "non-hot"/inactive, but they seem pretty active here
:::

## SVA transduction activity

:::{.center}
:::{.small}

![](./img/1kg_sv_lr-3a-sva.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}
![](./img/1kg_sv_lr-4b.png){fig-align="center" width="50%"}

:::
- SVAs are about 2-3kbp length elements
- Within element, there is bias for head/tail transduction, but across elements is well-distributed
- Greater reference agreement compared to L1 activity
- Subfamily is more entropic than L1
:::

## SVs in pop. future work

:::{.center}
- Joint seq-mechanism callers
- Variant prioritization
- Mobile element detection and inspection
:::

:::notes
- Leverage mechanistic models during call process rather than post-hoc annotation
- Use large SV callsets as background control to prioritize SVs driving disease. If frequent in these cohorts, unlikely to drive disease
- Mobile elements cause a significant amount of SVs, yet majority of callers focus on DELs and copy number variants
:::

## Driver mutations

![](./img/pcawg-2a.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Takeaway: severe cases have many types of SVs
- Takeaway 2 (bar): most patients have driver coding point mutation or SCNA (gene variants)
- angle separates samples
- outer:  sorted driver mutations per sample
- ii) Whole genome duplication presence (both homologous chromosomes are duplicated, could be just one pair)
- iii) Tumor type (color)
- iv) # driver CNVs
- v) # driver non-CNV rearrangements
- vi) # driver coding point mutations
- vii) # driver non-coding mutations
- viii) # Pathogenic germline variants
:::

## Gene driver variants

![](./img/pcawg-2b.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Notable: TP53 is most common driver mutation, TERT also common (telomere repair)
- Notable: cis-activating GR (GR=genomic rearrangement) prostate only ERG-TMPRSS2
- Notable: fusion BRAF in melanoma and CNS-piloastro
- Notable: many drivers deactivate tumor suppressing genes (TSG, light blue)
:::

## TSG DEL drivers

:::{.center}
TSG: tumor suppressor gene
:::

![](./img/pcawg-2c.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Bottom value: # patients w/ bi-allelic DEL DIV total # patients w/ somatic VAR in gene
- Notable: TP53 usually only heterozygous DEL
- Takeaway: homozgyous DEL is relatively uncommon compared to heterozgyous DELs
:::

## Missing driver investigation

:::{.center}
- 4/181 driver-free samples had >5% normal contamination
- DeTiN tool re-analyzed and found drivers
:::

![](./img/pcawg-3abc.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Takeaways: i) some samples' drivers were rescued after addressing tumor-in-normal contamination (a)
- Takeaways: 2) for TERT-sensitive cancers many samples depth and purity was estimated insufficient to detect TERT mutations (bc)
- a) contamination measured by variant allele frequency difference in tumor and normal
- b) Estimated mutation detection sensitivity given purity and depth
- Again, this was only done for samples w/o drivers
- c) TERT detection sensitivity in cancers where TERT is commonly mutated

:::

## Clustered variant events

![](./img/pcawg-4ab.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Takeaway a: Most kataaegis events were APOBEC3 type, except for lymphatic cancers
- Takeaway a: chromoplexy less common than kataegis
- Takeaway a: chromothripsis high variance across tumor types
- Takeaway b: neighboring kataegis events are rare, but some occur near driver genes
- b: radius inv prop to dist of kataegis events
- b: each dot is a kataegis event and its radial location is the distance to next event (sequential)
- APOBE3B-type means up-regulated
:::

## Chromoplexy and chromothripsis

:::notes
- Takeaway c: neighboring chromoplexy events are even more rare than kataegis events
  - Fewer dots in shaded region
- Takeaway d: chromothripsis events with smaller avg breakpoint in the SV cluster tend to cause CNV of driver genes
:::
